articles.title: One in five pregnancy airlift involves teenagers, exposes early marriage
articles.summary:
For 19-year-old Sushila Roka of ward 14 of Musikot Municipality in Rukum West, June 4 was supposed to be the day her family welcomed the arrival of her twins. Instead, it became a race against time.

As labour complications grew severe, the young mother-to-be was rushed to the district hospital. Doctors there delivered a distressing warning: the delay in reaching the facility had placed both Sushila and her unborn twins in serious danger.

“Prepare yourselves for the worst. She was not brought in on time, and we cannot save the babies,” Sushila’s sister-in-law Nandakala Roka recalled the doctors telling her.

A silence fell over the family.

Sushila was carrying twins. She went into labour at home, but as her condition worsened, her family brought her to the hospital. Doctors initially feared the worst, but after prolonged efforts, she delivered the first baby naturally. The second was delivered through an emergency Caesarean section.

The danger, however, was far from over.

Sushila developed severe postpartum haemorrhage. Doctors advised transferring her and her newborns to the provincial hospital, Surkhet. After receiving emergency clearance from the District Administration Office, a Nepali Army helicopter airlifted them to the provincial hospital.

“I don’t know if it was because she was so young, but even after delivery, the bleeding wouldn’t stop,” Nandakala said. “As her condition deteriorated, we panicked.”

Sushila’s case is not an exception.

On December 7, 15-year-old Karuna Bista of ward 2 of Jagannath Rural Municipality in Bajura delivered her baby after losing consciousness during labour.

Karuna passed out due to prolonged labour. By the time her family reached the district hospital, her condition had become critical.

After she suffered severe blood loss and developed complications, doctors referred her for advanced treatment.

“Perhaps because she was so young, my daughter-in-law passed out during labour,” said her mother-in-law Amrita Bista. “My grandson was born while she was completely unconscious.”

Karuna remained unresponsive for two days after giving birth. Following coordination between local and district authorities, an army helicopter airlifted her to provincial hospital, Surkhet for emergency treatment.

Fifteen-year-old Neelima Sherpa of ward 2 of Makalu Rural Municipality in Sankhuwasabha endured a similar ordeal.

On March 22, she was airlifted by army helicopter to Paropakar Maternity and Women’s Hospital in Thapathali, Kathmandu, after suffering life-threatening postpartum haemorrhage.

Neelima said she had no knowledge about pregnancy, childbirth, or risks involved because of her age.

“Instead of thinking about how I would deliver the baby, I was terrified about whether I would survive,” she recalled. “Becoming a mother for the first time under those circumstances was the most frightening moment of my life.”

She survived after relatives, local authorities and emergency services coordinated a free airlift.

But not every teenage mother survives.

The stories of Sushila, Karuna, and Neelima not only highlight Nepal’s weak healthcare infrastructure, but also reveal how deeply rooted child marriage and teenage pregnancy remain. Their experiences show the grave risks young mothers continue to face and the serious health and social consequences of early marriage and teenage pregnancy.

Reports on emergency helicopter evacuations, a critical lifeline for pregnant women in Nepal’s remote areas, show that 19 percent of women airlifted for pregnancy-related complications are teenagers.

Dr Sijan Rawal of Dolpa District Hospital said rural women face multiple barriers, including a lack of roads, ambulances, specialist doctors and adequately equipped health facilities.

“We lack paediatric specialists, essential life-support equipment and adequate medical manpower,” Rawal said.

Reaching health facilities from remote settlements itself is a major challenge. Many women are forced to give birth at home without skilled medical assistance because travelling to health centres can take hours or even days.

The difficult terrain and delayed access to care significantly increase the risks for both mothers and newborns.

Data from UNICEF Nepal show that child marriage remains widespread across the country. Karnali province has the highest rate of marriage before the age of 18, at 41 percent, while Bagmati has the lowest.

The rate stands at 24.2 percent in Koshi, 38.8 percent in Madhesh, 21.5 percent in Gandaki, 21.6 percent in Lumbini and 26 percent in Sudurpashchim. Records at the Karnali Province Health Directorate also show that teenage pregnancy remains persistently high in the region. The rate stood at 21.64 percent in the fiscal year 2022-23, before declining slightly to 20.64 percent in 2023-24. It then rose marginally to 20.82 percent in 2024-25 and reached 21.34 percent in 2025-26.

Dr Lalit Jung Shahi, a consultant gynaecologist and obstetrician in Karnali, said pregnancy among teenagers carries serious medical risks, particularly related to high blood pressure.

“Because teenagers face a higher risk of pre-eclampsia and hypertension, natural delivery is often unsafe,” Shahi said. “Teenagers brought to us through air rescue generally arrive with four major complications: severe bleeding before or after delivery, severe intrauterine growth restriction leading to low birth weight, acute hypertension and severe anaemia.”

Anju Dhungana, chief of the Women Empowerment Division at the Ministry of Women, Children, Gender and Sexual Minorities and Social Security, said all three levels of government must strengthen efforts to eliminate child marriage.

“Child marriage remains a major obstacle to Nepal’s human development,” Dhungana said. “We need sustained community-level awareness campaigns to educate adolescents about the serious physical and social consequences of early pregnancy.”

The government’s medical air rescue programme provides emergency evacuation for pregnant women and new mothers facing prolonged labour, severe complications or medical emergencies beyond the capacity of local health facilities.

According to the ministry, nearly 950 critically ill women from all seven provinces have so far received emergency air evacuation under the programme.

Under the President Woman Upliftment Programme, 54 critically ill pregnant women and new mothers from Karnali province were rescued free of charge in the last fiscal year alone.

Despite such interventions, maternal and newborn deaths remain a serious concern.

According to the Health Services Directorate, 11 women died from childbirth-related complications in Karnali in the last fiscal year, while 777 newborns have died in the province over the past four years.

Health workers say many women from remote areas reach health facilities only after complications have already become life-threatening, leaving emergency air rescue as the final option.

Reporting gaps weaken fight against child marriage

Despite laws banning child marriage, enforcement remains weak, largely because most cases never reach the authorities.

Stakeholders say families often settle cases within communities to avoid social stigma, family conflict and legal consequences, making official intervention difficult.

Nepal Police Deputy Inspector General Jayaraj Sapkota, chief of the Karnali Province Police Office, acknowledged that child marriage remains widespread but said the lack of formal complaints limits police action.

Rabi Raj Thapaliya, chief of police in Mugu, said the situation remains serious.

“Child marriage is widespread and the situation is grim,” Thapaliya said. “However, formal complaints are extremely rare because families try to avoid legal complications.”

According to DIG Sapkota, Karnali provincial police registered four child marriage cases in the fiscal year 2024-25, and all resulted in prosecution.

However, no formal complaint of child marriage had been filed anywhere in Karnali province in 2026, according to police data.

Social and systemic barriers keep the cycle alive

Child rights advocates and experts say child marriage and teenage pregnancy cannot be addressed through legal measures alone. They say progress will require improved access to education, healthcare and community-level enforcement. Nepal prohibits marriage before the age of 20, and those who arrange, conduct, or facilitate child marriage may face criminal penalties, including up to three years’ imprisonment and a fine of up to Rs30,000.

Child rights activist Tika Ram Acharya said many child marriages remain hidden, although some emerge during disputes over money or caste.

“Nearly 40 percent of young people in Karnali marry before reaching the legal age, according to estimates,” Acharya said. “The uncontrolled use of social media and the growing trend of live-in relationships among adolescents have also contributed to early marriages.”

He said families need stronger emotional support systems and better communication with teenagers.

“When young people do not find support at home, they often seek companionship and stability prematurely,” he said.

Sonam Bhuti Gurung, an activist from Kaike Rural Municipality in Dolpa who campaigns for girls’ education, said schools must provide stronger legal awareness.

“Remote areas face a double challenge: weak educational infrastructure and deep gender discrimination in access to schooling,” Gurung said. “Unless girls can continue to higher education, they will remain trapped in this cycle.”

She called for detailed research to identify communities where child marriage is most common.

“Lack of education and awareness encourages parents to marry off their daughters early,” she said. “When girls are denied education, marriage is seen as their only future.”

Kamala Tiwari, an associate professor at Mid-Western University in Surkhet, said policymakers often overlook the emotional vulnerabilities of adolescents.

“The state spends millions on campaigns against child marriage but fails to address the emotional needs of young people,” Tiwari said.

She said teenagers who marry early often face social pressure and legal uncertainty, making them reluctant to seek reproductive health services or use contraception.

“Instead of simply blaming young couples, we need to provide them with non-judgmental access to safe motherhood and reproductive healthcare,” she said.

Tiwari also pointed to legal complications created by Nepal’s marriage laws.

As Nepal outlaws child marriage, couples who marry below that age cannot legally register their marriages. As a result, many remain without official marriage records and may face difficulties accessing state benefits, birth certificates and social security services.

Fear of prosecution often pushes families to conceal early marriages and births, she said.

Tiwari identified hormonal changes during adolescence, digital exposure and a lack of open communication between parents and children as key factors behind early relationships.

She called for comprehensive life-skills and sexual health education in schools to help teenagers make informed decisions.

articles.title: Minister leads rescue of children in non-profit shelter
articles.summary:
A video of Minister for Women, Children and Senior Citizens Sita Badi breastfeeding a rescued infant went viral on Thursday evening, July 23, drawing widespread public attention and praise for what many described as an act of maternal compassion.

The child in the video, however, was not Badi’s own son. The 17-day-old girl was among 20 children rescued on Saturday, July 18, from a shelter home operated by the Nepal Children’s Organisation (NCO) at Bal Mandir in Naxal, Kathmandu, after concerns were raised over their living conditions.

“When I took it in my arms, I saw my own child in her. Before I realised it, tears welled in my eyes,” Badi told Kantipur.

Badi, who often takes her 19-month-old son to ministry meetings and public events, said the incident had a deeply personal connection for her. She herself spent part of her childhood in a care home.

“I never imagined I would become a parliamentarian or a minister,” she said. “When I got this portfolio unexpectedly, it felt like I could give it a personal touch.”

The moment captured in the viral video was of Sunday, July 19, a day after Badi ordered the evacuation of 20 children under two years from the non-government organisation’s central office.

The children, including 12 boys and eight girls aged between 15 days and two years, were moved after reports of deteriorating conditions at the facility during the monsoon.

The rescue team included representatives from the minister’s secretariat, the Kathmandu Metropolitan City Ward 1, the KMC Child Rescue Task Force, the KMC Child Rights Committee and personnel from Maligaun Police Circle.

The intervention came after a social media user commented on one of Badi’s posts, urging her to inspect Bal Mandir during the rainy season. After her secretariat brought the comment to her attention, Badi made an unannounced visit to the facility.

She said she was disturbed by what she saw, including children in unclean clothes and with runny noses, and issued written instructions to the management to improve conditions immediately.

The situation drew further attention last week after Rasala Tandukar, a ward member of KMC-1, posted photographs showing poor conditions inside the care centre and warned that the health and wellbeing of the children were at risk.

After seeing the photographs, Badi ordered an emergency evacuation during heavy rainfall. At around 6 pm on Saturday, July 18, a rescue team reached Bal Mandir.

“Sewage had entered the room where infants below two years were kept, forcing staff to move them to an administrative office,” said Soni Bhattarai, a personal secretary to the minister who took part in the rescue.

“Twenty infants were placed on a single floor mat, and dry instant noodles had been scattered in front of them,” she said.

Ramesh Roka, another personal secretary involved in the operation, said NCO chairperson Bidya Neupane initially objected to the evacuation, alleging that officials were trying to shut down the organisation.

“Given the condition of the facility, we could not leave the children there,” Roka said. “Seeing two infants smile in my arms after we boarded the rescue vehicle was an emotional moment.”

After the evacuation, Badi held an emergency meeting with ministry officials to arrange resources for temporary care. On Sunday evening, July 19, she visited the shelter with a medical team led by Dr Ramji Ram.

Medical examinations found several children suffering from eye infections, skin problems and severe cough. While doctors examined the children, Badi helped clean and bathe the infants.

During the visit, a 17-day-old child began crying and did not stop. As the shelter had no formula milk or other feeding options, Badi held the child and breastfed him until he calmed down and fell asleep.

“It felt as though this child had been deprived of nourishment for a long time,” Bhattarai recalled telling the minister.

“I am his mother now,” Badi replied.

Five caregivers have since been assigned to the temporary shelter, with each responsible for four children.

“Although these arrangements were made on an emergency basis without a separate payroll budget, the children’s health has improved significantly,” Badi said, adding that she breastfed the child twice that evening.

She rejected allegations that the intervention was aimed at dissolving the NCO.

“We have no intention of shutting down the organisation, nor do we have any hostility towards anyone. Our only objective is to ensure proper care for these children,” she said.

Badi said the current arrangement was temporary and that the government-owned land where NCO operates should have been better managed.

“NCO sits on government property. Had the infrastructure been properly maintained, this crisis could have been avoided,” she said.

The ministry is monitoring construction of a new building at the premises, which is expected to be completed within four months, she added.

Badi also said the ministry was working to address long-standing problems faced by children without parental care, including difficulties obtaining citizenship certificates. She proposed a sustainable funding mechanism for child welfare through small voluntary contributions from civil servants’ salaries.

NCO central chairperson Bidya Neupane said flooding at the facility was caused by blocked drainage and construction-related debris. She blamed delays by contractors for leaving renovation work on the main building incomplete despite an original completion deadline in the fiscal year 2021/22.

Neupane said staff had already begun shifting children to safer areas within the compound before the government team arrived.

“Protecting children is the state’s responsibility, and I view the ministry’s intervention positively,” she said.

Prabin Silwal, a member of the KMC Child Rights Committee who participated in the rescue, said municipal authorities had repeatedly worked to address drainage problems in the area.

“Continuous heavy rainfall for two days, combined with ongoing renovation work, created unsafe conditions that made immediate relocation necessary,” Silwal said.

He added that the KMC and the NCO were coordinating to implement standard operating procedures for child care homes across the metropolis.

articles.title: From SLR rifles to DSLR cameras
articles.summary:
For 26 years, Sudeep KC trained his eyes on targets through the iron sights of an SLR rifle. Today, he uses the same discipline and precision to frame wildlife through the viewfinder of a camera.

The 58-year-old former Nepali Army colonel has spent the past seven years documenting Nepal’s birds, mammals and landscapes, transforming a military skill set built on patience, observation and accuracy into a career in wildlife photography.

His ability to locate elusive species, work in difficult terrain and capture wildlife in challenging conditions has earned him recognition among nature enthusiasts in Nepal and abroad. International photographers now travel to Nepal seeking his guidance on tracking wildlife and photographing species in their natural habitats.

A resident of Basundhara in Tokha Municipality-5, Kathmandu, KC retired from the army after a 26-year career and turned to wildlife photography full-time in 2019.

His interest in conservation began much earlier, during military postings to national parks where army units were deployed for security operations. Working alongside park officials, conservationists and nature guides introduced him to Nepal’s biodiversity and deepened his interest in wildlife.

Since taking up photography professionally, KC has photographed 595 bird species in Nepal.

“I have sighted more than 630 bird species in the wild,” KC told Kantipur. “But because of timing, weather conditions and physical limitations, I have not been able to photograph all of them.”

Nepal has officially recorded 903 bird species.

KC’s search for rare species has also taken him beyond Nepal. During photography expeditions to Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand, he documented 378 bird species, many of which are not found in Nepal.

Among his most memorable achievements is photographing the Himalayan Monal, Nepal’s national bird.

“Capturing a clear image of the Monal required the greatest effort and persistence,” KC said. “I had been tracking the bird for a long time.”

He photographed the colourful pheasant at an altitude of 2,600 metres inside Shivapuri-Nagarjun National Park, and believes he was the first wildlife photographer to capture the species within the Kathmandu Valley.

“We had walked through dense forest for nearly four hours and were completely exhausted,” he recalled. “Just as we were about to turn back disappointed, the bird appeared right in front of us. Others with me also saw it, but I managed to frame and capture it first.”

From the Tarai plains to the Himalayas

KC spends three to four months every year travelling across Nepal in search of wildlife, moving from the grasslands of the Tarai to the high-altitude landscapes of the Himalayas.

When in Kathmandu, he regularly visits local wetlands, ridgelines and forest patches to photograph birds.

His portfolio includes grassland species, migratory winter and summer visitors, forest birds and farmland species. He has photographed the Spiny Babbler, believed to be Nepal’s only endemic bird species, as well as rare sightings such as the Mandarin Duck.

Beyond birds, KC has documented 25 species of mammals and reptiles, including the Royal Bengal tiger, sloth bear, leopard, one-horned rhinoceros, Asian elephant, spotted deer, barking deer, blackbuck, otter, Gangetic dolphin and Indian python.

Since beginning wildlife photography, he has encountered 12 wild tigers, successfully photographing most of them.

“I prefer photographing tigers in their natural habitat rather than taking close-up portraits,” he said. “Habitat photography requires patience, tracking skills and long hours in the field. The excitement of seeing a tiger in dense forest never disappears.”

He recalled following tiger footprints for four days inside Bardiya National Park before capturing an image of an adult tiger crossing a river at Tinkune, Bardiya.

But wildlife photography has also brought moments of danger.

“While on a full-day jungle walk with ornithologist Ram Shahi in Bardiya, a full-grown tiger appeared on the trail just three to four metres ahead of us,” KC said. “Adrenaline took over. Instead of raising the camera, our first instinct was to find safety.”

Two hours later, when they spotted the same tiger from a safer distance, KC said his hands were still shaking.

In another encounter in Sukebar, Chitwan, he had to climb a tree after unexpectedly coming across a one-horned rhinoceros.

Photographing the elusive Red Panda in the snow-covered forests of Nanggin Got inside Langtang National Park required waiting in freezing conditions for three consecutive days.

“Wildlife photography demands immense patience,” KC said. “Every second matters. You have to move quietly, understand animal behaviour and capture angles that make your work different.”

His assignments have taken him to more than 40 districts across Nepal, from the plains of the Tarai to Upper Dolpa.

Guiding international photographers

KC’s wildlife photographs shared on social media have attracted international photographers interested in Nepal’s biodiversity.

“Two months ago, a group of four Japanese photographers visited Nepal,” he said. “I guided them to key habitats where they successfully photographed several native bird and mammal species.”

Two years ago, KC was appointed Nepal Country Representative for the Asian Wildlife Photography Club (AWPC).

Through the organisation, he leads annual photography tours for visitors from Singapore, Malaysia, India and Sri Lanka to biodiversity hotspots including Chitwan, Bardiya and the Kathmandu Valley.

“When visiting photographers capture high-quality images here and display them abroad, it helps promote Nepal’s ecotourism,” KC said. “Nepal has rich wildlife resources that can attract nature enthusiasts from around the world.”

His photographs have been featured in calendars, brochures and books published by the National Trust for Nature Conservation, Bird Conservation Nepal, the Nepal Tourism Board and international journals.

KC sees a strong connection between his military training and photography.

“In both disciplines, you aim with one eye, stabilise your body, hold your breath and act at the right moment without shaking,” he said. “In the army, we use camouflage and concealment so the target does not detect us. In wildlife photography, camouflage helps prevent disturbing animals.”

“Pulling the trigger of a rifle fires a bullet; pressing the shutter of a camera captures an image.”

From soldier to conservationist

KC’s photographs of landscapes, cultural heritage and rural life have won recognition in national competitions.

In 2025, he secured first place and a cash prize of Rs50,000 in the non-military category of a national photography competition organised by the Nepal Army. Three years earlier, he won second prize in a national contest organised by Kia Motors.

KC joined the Nepal Army as a Second Lieutenant in 1990, with his first posting at Chitwan National Park.

Working alongside park staff, conservationists and nature guides sparked his interest in wildlife tracking and species identification.

In 1991, he participated in the translocation of four one-horned rhinoceroses from Chitwan to Bardiya National Park.

“Before joining the military, I had a general interest in birdwatching,” he said. “My time in Chitwan deepened that interest. During long patrols, I carried binoculars and field guides to identify species along the trail.”

After two years in Chitwan, KC was transferred to Kathmandu, where he served for more than 12 years as a close protection officer for the royal family. During royal visits to Bardiya and Chitwan, he often informally guided visitors on wildlife.

Following the 2001 royal palace incident, KC was posted to Bardiya National Park as a major, commanding an army company responsible for park security during the Maoist conflict.

“Operating from national park barracks during the conflict brought different challenges,” he said. “We had to secure our positions, protect military assets and safeguard wildlife from poachers at the same time.”

During his military career, KC spent more than 14 years stationed in protected areas, including Shey-Phoksundo National Park, Rara National Park and Parsa Wildlife Reserve, now Parsa National Park.

While commanding forces in Bardiya, he led anti-poaching operations in coordination with park authorities.

In 2011-12, joint operations in the Surkhet-Barahatal buffer zone recovered 242 illegal muzzle-loading firearms.

Later, in 2015, during a military health camp in Upper Dolpa, his unit confiscated illegally stored snow leopard pelts based on local intelligence.

The photographer’s tools

KC began his photography journey with a Canon 6D Mark II paired with a 150-600mm zoom lens.

After consulting international wildlife photographers, he upgraded his equipment.

He now uses a Sony Alpha 1 camera body, valued at around Rs900,000, with a 100-400mm G Master zoom lens worth approximately Rs350,000.

The equipment, he says, allows him to capture fast-moving wildlife with improved autofocus tracking and high-speed shutter performance.

For KC, however, the most important tools remain the ones he developed long before he picked up a camera: patience, discipline and the ability to wait for the right moment.

articles.title: क्लिन, ग्रिन एन्ड रिलायबल ऊर्जालाई क्षेत्रीय बजारमा विस्तार गर्न निजी क्षेत्रको सहभागिता आवश्यक
articles.summary:
ऊर्जा, जलस्रोत तथा सिँचाइ मन्त्री विराज भक्त श्रेष्ठले नेपालको स्वच्छ, हरित र भरपर्दो (क्लिन, ग्रिन एन्ड रिलायबल) ऊर्जालाई क्षेत्रीय बजारमा प्रतिस्पर्धी रूपमा विस्तार गर्न विद्युत व्यापारमा निजी क्षेत्रको सहभागिता आवश्यक बन्दै गएको बताएका छन् ।

उनले यसका लागि विद्यमान कानुनी व्यवस्थाले पर्याप्त आधार दिन्छ वा नयाँ कानुन आवश्यक पर्छ भन्ने विषयमा सरकारले सकारात्मक रूपमा अध्ययन गरिरहेको बताए ।

शुक्रबार स्वतन्त्र ऊर्जा उत्पादकहरुको संस्था नेपाल (इप्पान) का पदाधिकारीसँग मन्त्रालयमा भएको छलफलमा मन्त्री श्रेष्ठले विद्युत उत्पादनमा निजी क्षेत्रको उल्लेखनीय योगदान रहे पनि व्यापारको क्षेत्रमा अझै पर्याप्त अवसर खुल्न नसकेको उल्लेख गरे ।

बदलिँदो ऊर्जा बजार र क्षेत्रीय विद्युत व्यापारको सम्भावनालाई मध्यनजर गर्दै निजी क्षेत्रको सहभागिताबारे समयानुकूल निर्णय लिन आवश्यक देखिएको उनको भनाइ छ ।

मन्त्री श्रेष्ठले निजी क्षेत्रलाई नेपाल विद्युत प्राधिकरणसँग समन्वय गरेर ‘बिजनेस–टु–बिजनेस (बी–टु–बी)’ मोडलमार्फत अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय बजार खोज्न आवश्यक अनुमति प्रदान गर्ने विषयमा आफू सकारात्मक रहेको जानकारी दिए ।

ऊर्जा खपत तथा निर्यात रणनीति कार्यान्वयनको चरणमा रहेको वर्तमान अवस्थामा विद्युत व्यापार निजी क्षेत्रका लागि नयाँ लगानी र व्यावसायिक अवसर बन्न सक्ने उनको भनाइ थियो ।

उनले निजी क्षेत्रलाई व्यापारमा सहभागी गराउँदा नेपाल विद्युत प्राधिकरणको भूमिका, अधिकार र जिम्मेवारी सुरक्षित रहनुपर्ने तथा राज्यले प्राप्त गर्ने प्रतिफलमा कुनै असर नपर्ने व्यवस्था सुनिश्चित गर्नुपर्नेमा जोड दिए ।

खुला पहुँच (ओपन एक्सेस) प्रणाली, साझा प्रसारण पूर्वाधारको उपयोग, दायित्व बाँडफाँट तथा विद्युत व्यापारको डिजिटल व्यवस्थापनजस्ता विषयमा पनि विस्तृत अध्ययन आवश्यक रहेको उनले उल्लेख गरे ।

मन्त्री श्रेष्ठले ऊर्जा क्षेत्रको विस्तारले मुलुकको कुल गार्हस्थ्य उत्पादन (जीडीपी) मा उल्लेखनीय योगदान पुर्याउने विश्वास व्यक्त गर्दै अर्थतन्त्रलाई एक सय खर्ब रुपैयाँको आकारमा पुर्याउने राष्ट्रिय लक्ष्यमा ऊर्जा क्षेत्र निर्णायक बन्न सक्ने बताए ।

articles.title: नेपालमा अपाङ्गता भएका व्यक्तिको वित्तीय पहुँच अझै कमजोर
articles.summary:
नेपालमा अपाङ्गता भएका व्यक्तिहरूको वित्तीय समावेशीकरण अझै पनि कमजोर रहेको र कानुनी तथा नीतिगत व्यवस्था भएपनि प्रभावकारी कार्यान्वयन हुन नसकेको एक अध्ययनले देखाएको छ ।

सीबीएम ग्लोबलले सप्रोस, अपाङ्ग महिला संघ तथा अन्य साझेदार संस्थासँगको सहकार्यमा तयार गरेको ‘नेपालमा अपाङ्गता भएका व्यक्तिहरूको वित्तीय समावेशीकरण सम्बन्धी अध्ययन प्रतिवेदन शुक्रबार ललितपुरमा सार्वजनिक गरिएको हो ।

अध्ययनले अपाङ्गता भएका व्यक्तिहरूको बैंक तथा वित्तीय सेवामा पहुँच, सेवा प्रयोग र समावेशीकरणको वर्तमान अवस्थाको विश्लेषण गर्दै वित्तीय प्रणालीमा रहेका संरचनागत, नीतिगत र व्यवहारगत कमजोरीहरू औंल्याएको छ।

साथै वित्तीय समावेशीकरणलाई प्रभावकारी बनाउन आवश्यक नीतिगत सुधार, संस्थागत व्यवस्था तथा कार्यान्वयनका लागि विभिन्न सिफारिस पनि प्रस्तुत गरिएको छ।

कार्यक्रममा प्रयत्न नेपालीकी अध्यक्ष सरिता लामिछानेले अपाङ्गता भएका व्यक्तिहरूको अधिकारसम्बन्धी महासन्धि, अपाङ्गता अधिकार ऐन तथा नेपाल राष्ट्र बैंकका विभिन्न नीतिगत व्यवस्था भएपनि तिनको कार्यान्वयन पक्ष निकै कमजोर रहेको बताइन्।
